analysis.one_liner: Strips the lesser prairie-chicken of all Endangered Species Act protection, permanently.
analysis.headline: The delisting bill, introduced by Senator Marshall with four Republican cosponsors, has sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing or vote since January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill takes the lesser prairie-chicken, a grassland bird in the Southern Great Plains, off the endangered and threatened species lists entirely. It also writes a permanent exemption into the Endangered Species Act itself so that the federal government can never list or protect this bird again, no matter what happens to its population.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas drillers, wind and solar developers, and farmers and ranchers across the Southern Great Plains would gain, because Endangered Species Act protection for the prairie-chicken triggers federal reviews and land-use restrictions on activities in its habitat. Removing the bird from the lists and barring any future listing clears that work out of the way permanently.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Energy and farm interests on prairie habitat

how_it_helps.text: Removes the lesser prairie-chicken from the federal threatened and endangered species lists, ending the permitting reviews, land-use restrictions, and potential liability that ESA protection imposes on projects and land management in its habitat.

Amends the Endangered Species Act itself to permanently prohibit the Fish and Wildlife Service from ever listing the bird again, giving landowners and developers in the five-state habitat region certainty that no future administration can reverse course.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the loss of federal protection for the lesser prairie-chicken: no recovery plan, no mandatory review of projects in its habitat, and no legal path to ever protect it again, even if its numbers keep falling. The cost is paid by the species itself and by Americans who value keeping it from going extinct.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes every federal safeguard for the lesser prairie-chicken and, unlike a normal delisting that can be revisited with new data, makes it illegal to ever protect the bird again, even if the science later shows its population collapsing.

An Endangered Species Act listing is the tool the government uses when a species is heading toward extinction; deleting the bird from the act's authority means that if voluntary conservation efforts fall short, there is no federal backstop and the risk of losing the species falls on the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: lower compliance costs and fewer permitting hurdles for energy, wind, and farm operations on prairie habitat in a handful of Great Plains states. The cost is that a grassland bird already in steep decline would lose its only federal safety net, and the bill goes further than any ordinary delisting would by barring future protection by law. The permanence is the problem: it forecloses the option to act later, whatever the evidence shows.

outcome.mechanism: It was read once in the Senate and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote ever since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 21, 2025 and, under Senate practice, was read twice and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee without debate.
It has four cosponsors, all Republicans from states with prairie-chicken habitat or energy interests: Senators Lankford, Mullin, and Moran alongside sponsor Marshall.
No hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has come out ahead: the species keeps its current federal protection and the energy and agricultural interests the bill was written for have gained nothing. The bill is waiting in committee with no signs of movement.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill hasn't moved

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its permanent delisting language

for.name: Sens. James Lankford, Markwayne Mullin, and Jerry Moran

sides.party_line_note: All five senators behind the bill are Republicans from Great Plains states; no Democrat has supported it, and no vote has occurred.

industries.note: Prairie-chicken habitat overlays active oil and gas country in Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, and New Mexico. Listing under the Endangered Species Act requires federal review of projects that could harm the bird; this bill would remove that review and make it impossible to restore.

Wind farms and transmission lines in prairie-chicken habitat face ESA permitting and siting constraints. Delisting would free developers from those reviews, at the cost of the bird's federal protection.

A listing can restrict grazing, plowing, and brush control on private rangeland designated as critical habitat, which many landowners and state officials opposed. Some of the same landowners benefit from voluntary conservation funding tied to the bird's status, so the interest is not uniform.

analysis.trajectory: With only five Republican sponsors, no hearing, and no action in the Environment and Public Works Committee for a year, the bill is unlikely to reach the Senate floor on its own. The realistic path, if any, is attachment to a broader bill — such as an energy or appropriations package — where a species delisting could ride along; otherwise it will sit in committee until the Congress ends.
